title: 3-Read Friday #118: AI in Schools, Scaffolding, and Wait Time
author: Craig Barton
summary: 3-Read Friday #118 opens with Joel Kenyon's dystopian vision of education in 2045 -- AI deepfake teachers trained on real staff, classes of 250, and human teachers reduced to minimum-wage behaviour monitors -- built to make the point that when cost-cutting drives edtech adoption, the relationship at the heart of teaching is the first casualty. Dominic Salles then argues that scaffolding becomes the enemy of hard thinking unless its removal is planned from the start, contending that tasks should stay simple while thinking should be complex from minute one, and suggesting we've misread Rosenshine's 80% success-rate guidance along the way. Jonathan Nicolas Jarrett-Kerr closes by making the case for wait time as one of the most inclusive things a teacher can do specifically because it is so hard to hold your nerve through the silence, arguing it applies well beyond questioning into whiteboards and quizzes too. Barton frames the Kenyon piece as the one that stuck with him all week despite his own general enthusiasm for AI in education.
points: Kenyon's 2045 scenario is a deliberate warning, not a prediction: when cost-cutting is what actually drives edtech adoption, the human relationship at the center of teaching is the first thing sacrificed.

Salles's scaffolding critique: unless removal is planned from the outset, scaffolding becomes a substitute for hard thinking rather than a bridge to it -- tasks should stay simple while the thinking demanded stays complex from the start.
Salles also challenges a common misreading of Rosenshine's 80% success-rate guidance, suggesting it's been used to justify exactly the kind of over-scaffolding it wasn't meant to license.

Jarrett-Kerr's wait-time argument extends past verbal questioning into whiteboards and quizzes, framing wait time as inclusive precisely because holding the silence is uncomfortable for the teacher, not because it's easy.
quotes: I love AI, and I'm genuinely excited about what it could do for teaching, which is exactly why a dystopian vision of it all going wrong has stuck with me all week.
